name: Sam Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck at the Red Hill copper pit, a Cat 793, which is basically a two-storey house on wheels. Shift starts at six, we do the pre-start checks, then I'm going round and round between the shovel and the crusher for twelve hours, about forty loads on a good day. I like the quiet up in the cab and I like the crew. What wears me out is the night roster, seven nights on, and the dust in summer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's the crew, and what's life like off shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My friend Dario runs the shovel, and he's the reason I'm still sane on nights, we talk on the radio about football. I rent a two-bedroom place on Station Road in Marrow Creek with my girlfriend, Lena, who works at the pharmacy. Money's tight, honestly. I'm on the bottom of the operator pay scale because I came over from a contractor, and there's a car loan, so there's maybe two weeks of bills in the bank at any time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like what I already believe. Every few years someone in a suit comes up from head office with a new system and in six months we're back to doing it the old way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, probably in the crib room, which is what we call the lunch hut. Something like, see, they spent millions on the computer and the trucks still need Sam. Online I don't really post much, maybe a comment on the union page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my job, which is all I want right now. But I'm not stupid, the company still wants to squeeze us, AI or no AI. If it's not robots it'll be a new roster or cutting the dust allowance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep turning up, keep paying my union dues, and try to get the car loan down before the end of next year. Maybe ask for a step up the pay scale at the next review, since I've been here four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's the world I know, and I'd take that. There's a little bit of me that would still be watching the north pit, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's in the north pit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They trialled three driverless trucks up there last year. They run off GPS and a control room in the city, two thousand kilometres away. Officially it was a trial, but nobody's told us it's over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing radical changes, does that trial just go away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In this picture, I think it sits there half-done like everything else. The trucks kept stopping for a stray dog or a bit of dust on the sensor and someone had to drive out and reset them. My dad would've laughed, he always said machines are only as smart as the guy who fixes them.

S0.say: He'd tell the crib room he called it: the company spent millions on computers and the trucks still need a driver. He might drop a comment on the union page but doesn't post much.
S0.think: He thinks his job is safe in this picture but the company will keep looking for other ways to squeeze the crew. He still keeps one eye on the driverless trucks trialled in the north pit.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal and keeps paying union dues. Tries to pay down the car loan by the end of next year and asks for a step up the pay scale at his next review.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, with a small background worry about the driverless truck trial.
S0.quote: See, they spent millions on the computer and the trucks still need Sam.
S0.fieldNote: Sam starts from deep scepticism about head office technology, and this scenario confirms his view of the world. Even in the calmest picture, he frames the company as the one who'll squeeze workers. The north pit trial sits in the back of his mind and comes up unprompted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's closer to home. Haul trucks are the first thing they'd go after, everyone knows that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd be loud about it. I'd be telling the crew to get to the union meeting and saying the company owes us a plan, not a farewell barbecue. Online I'd share whatever the union puts out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'm the exact kind of worker that shrinks. I'm average, I drive a truck, I've got a certificate and that's it. If they cut drivers from forty to fifteen, I'm not sure I'm in the fifteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd ask Dario how he got onto the shovel, because they'll keep shovel operators longer. I'd cancel the streaming and the gym and start putting fifty a fortnight away, which is about all I can do. And I'd go to every union meeting and push for a no-forced-redundancies deal before the trucks arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest, if I'm honest. It's not the end of the world, but it's the end of my bit of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned learning the shovel. Would you use any of the new tools, the AI ones, to get ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I don't touch that stuff, Lena uses it to write emails and I just watch. I'd rather learn the shovel off Dario the proper way, sitting next to him on a night shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lena say if you came home and told her drivers were being cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say we'll be fine, because she always does. Then she'd go quiet and start looking at jobs in the city, which is the bit I'd hate. I don't want to leave Marrow Creek, my mum's here and so's everything I know.

S1.say: He'd be loud at work, telling the crew to get to union meetings and saying the company owes them a plan. Online he'd share whatever the union puts out.
S1.think: He believes average truck drivers like him are exactly who gets cut, and he isn't sure he'd survive a cut from forty drivers to fifteen. He sees moving onto the shovel as his best chance of staying on.
S1.do: Asks his shovel-operator friend how to get trained on the shovel and cancels streaming and the gym to save about fifty a fortnight. Goes to every union meeting to push for a no-forced-redundancies deal before the driverless trucks come.
S1.feel: A tight chest; not the end of the world, but the end of his part of it.
S1.quote: The company owes us a plan, not a farewell barbecue.
S1.fieldNote: Even a moderate change lands hard for Sam because his job is the obvious target and his savings are thin. He wants to learn the next skill the old way, from a friend on nights, and refuses AI tools outright. His biggest dread is not the job loss itself but being pushed out of Marrow Creek.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's two more Christmases. I don't even know what to say to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a crime and the government should stop it. I'd be the one at the gate with the sign, and I'd be posting for the first time in my life, telling people to ring their member of parliament.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished in this job, and probably in this town. Driverless trucks already half work, so with real AGI they'd be in by the first year. There's nothing else here that pays rent except the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd sell the car and get something cheap, so the loan's gone. I'd go to the union and push for a strike or at least a big payout for every driver, and I'd sign up for whatever government support there is the day it opens. Lena and I would probably have to move in with my mum for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like the moment the truck slides on a wet ramp and you can't do anything about it. Two years isn't enough time to learn anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said two years isn't enough to learn anything. What would you want to learn, if there were time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that's the problem. If robots are doing hands-on work too, then electrician's out, mechanic's out. I'd be learning something for a job that's gone by the time I finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies building it and the mining company buying it. They'll save a fortune on wages and none of it comes back to Marrow Creek. The government should be taxing the robots and paying the towns, and I'd vote for whoever says so out loud.

S2.say: He'd call it a crime, stand at the mine gate with a sign, and post online for the first time, urging people to call their member of parliament. He wants the government to step in.
S2.think: He privately believes he's finished as a driver and probably in his town too, since driverless trucks already half work. Nothing else in Marrow Creek pays rent like the mine.
S2.do: Sells the car to clear the loan, pushes the union for a strike or a big payout for every driver, and signs up for government support the day it opens. Plans to move in with his mum with his girlfriend for a while.
S2.feel: Sick and helpless, like a truck sliding on a wet ramp, with no time to learn anything new.
S2.quote: Like the moment the truck slides on a wet ramp and you can't do anything about it. Two years isn't enough time to learn anything.
S2.fieldNote: With two years of warning, Sam runs out of moves: no savings, no other local work and no interest in new tools. His answer is all collective: the union, the gate, the ballot box. He blames the tech companies and the mining company, and wants robots taxed to pay towns like his.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit different. Still fast, but you'd see the trucks coming up the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, that the union needs to get in early. With five years there's time for a real deal: retraining money, guaranteed jobs in the control room, a payout for anyone left over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years scares me in a different way. With two years everyone's in the same mess. With five, the smart ones get out early and the ones like me who hate change get left holding the shovel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get on the union committee, which I've always said I'd do and never have. I'd try to save a bit more, maybe pick up extra shifts while there's still overtime. And I'd vote and campaign for anyone promising a robot tax for mining towns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, losing sleep worried. But at least there's something to do with my hands, if you know what I mean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between year one and year five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd be at meetings and doing overtime. By year three I'd be watching the first driverless trucks come in for real, probably on the nights first, because nobody wants nights. By year five I'd be fighting for my spot or fighting for my payout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the ones who hate change get left. Would that be you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah. I know myself. I'll be the last guy still saying the old way works, right up until the day it doesn't.

S3.say: He'd say the union must get in early and use the five years to win a real deal: retraining money, control-room jobs and payouts for anyone left over.
S3.think: He fears five years splits the workforce: the quick ones get out early while people like him, who resist change, get left behind. He admits he'll be the last to give up the old way.
S3.do: Joins the union committee, picks up overtime while it's still there to save a little, and campaigns and votes for a robot tax for mining towns.
S3.feel: Worried enough to lose sleep, but steadier because there's something practical to do.
S3.quote: With five, the smart ones get out early and the ones like me who hate change get left holding the shovel.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years don't make Sam feel safer; they make him see his own resistance to change as the danger. He turns to organising rather than retraining. He was honest that he'd be the last to let go of the old way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole other life, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse this time. If the company and the government know it's coming for ten years and still leave towns like ours with nothing, that's a choice, not an accident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years is enough time for me to do something I'd normally never do, which is train for something. I'd hate it, but I'd have to. I'm not sure what's left by 2036, though, so I'd be guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd still be driving and saving what I can, and I'd sit down with the union to get the company to pay for courses. I'd probably start a maintenance or electrical ticket part-time, because someone has to fix the robots, at least for a while. I'd stay on the committee the whole way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe. It's still the same ending, though, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate retraining. What would that look like in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Night classes at the tech college in Bellmont, an hour's drive, after a twelve-hour shift. I failed maths at school, so I'd be the oldest one in the room asking dumb questions. But Lena would push me, she'd probably print the forms herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the ten years change how you think about staying in Marrow Creek?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does a bit. With ten years I might be able to save enough to stay, or the town might find something else. With two years I'd just be gone.

S4.say: He'd say there's no excuse this time: if the company and government have ten years' warning and still leave mining towns with nothing, that's a choice.
S4.think: He thinks ten years is enough to force himself to retrain, even though he'd hate it. He isn't sure which jobs will be left by 2036, so any choice feels like a guess.
S4.do: Keeps driving and saving while pressing the union to get the company to pay for courses. Starts a part-time maintenance or electrical course at the tech college an hour away and stays on the union committee throughout.
S4.feel: Uneasy but able to breathe, while knowing the ending is still the same.
S4.quote: If the company and the government know it's coming for ten years and still leave towns like ours with nothing, that's a choice, not an accident.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years is the only picture where Sam talks about retraining for himself, and only with pressure from his girlfriend and the union paying. He still rates the threat as serious because the end point is the same and his savings stay thin. The extra time mainly gives him hope of staying in his town.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Two years and I'm out with nothing. What would help is a proper payout and wages paid while we train, funded by the companies that save all that money, and someone actually coming to Marrow Creek to ask what the town needs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my dad. He drove trucks at Red Hill before me, and when he retired they gave him a watch. I'd just like to get to the watch, that's all.

headlineQuote: My dad would've laughed, he always said machines are only as smart as the guy who fixes them.
portrait: Sam Reyes is a 27-year-old haul truck driver at the Red Hill copper pit, renting with his girlfriend Lena in Marrow Creek, with about two weeks of bills in the bank and a car loan. He's a union man, distrusts head-office technology and never uses AI tools. A slow picture leaves him calm, but steady change makes him anxious because truck drivers are the first target. AGI in two years leaves him panicked with no moves left except the union and the ballot box, and even ten years only pushes him reluctantly towards night classes. Throughout, he blames the tech and mining companies and wants a robot tax that pays towns like his.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years would leave him out of work with nothing to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: A proper payout and wages paid while training, funded by the companies that save the money, and someone coming to Marrow Creek to ask what the town needs.
